summary: Defines the ACCEPT_OWN BGP community attribute. A route reflector can modify the Route Target list of a VPN route so that a route originated in one VRF can be accepted by another VRF on the originating router.

plainLanguage.summary: A special sticker that tells a router, you may accept this one even though it came from you.

questions: why does bgp reject its own routes
subtitle: A BGP community that lets a router accept a route it originated itself, so a route reflector can steer routes between VRFs on the same router.

tldr.problem: A route reflector can change the Route Target list of a VPN route to control import into other VRFs, but this fails when the exporting and importing VRFs are on the same PE, because BGP rejects routes that a speaker originated itself.
tldr.mechanism: A new well-known community, ACCEPT_OWN (0xFFFF0001), lets a router accept such a route when it is enabled by configuration, targets a different VRF on the router, and the route's Route Distinguisher matches a local source VRF.
tldr.outcome: Route reflectors can apply the same Route Target rewriting everywhere in an autonomous system, whether or not the VRFs share a PE.

facts.label: Community type
facts.value: Well-known, First Come First Served range

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: One AS, single layer of route reflectors

today: RFC 7611 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015. The metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
A BGP speaker may maintain several VRFs (VPN Routing and Forwarding tables, see RFC 4364). Sometimes a route reflector should change the Route Target (RT) list of a VPN route it distributes, so that it controls how a route originated in one VRF is imported into others. Doing this on the originating router is possible, but may be operationally cumbersome in an autonomous system with many border routers and complex BGP policies.

The technique works as long as the exporting VRF is not on the same Provider Edge (PE) router as the importing VRF. If they share a PE it fails, because under RFC 4271 a BGP speaker rejects advertisements that it originated. The route reflector attaches an ORIGINATOR_ID so the originator can spot such routes, and a route should not be accepted from a peer whose NEXT_HOP equals the receiver's own address.
sections.plainLanguage: A router normally ignores its own mail when it comes back. That is a problem if the mail was meant for another desk in the same office.

sections.title: The ACCEPT_OWN Community
sections.content:
The RFC defines ACCEPT_OWN, a new well-known BGP community (RFC 1997) in the First Come First Served range, with the value 0xFFFF0001 assigned by IANA. Processing it SHOULD be controlled by configuration and SHOULD default to disabled.

The goal is to let the RT-list technique be used in a standard way throughout an autonomous system, whether or not the VRFs are on the same PE.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker has a fixed shape everywhere, so every router reads it the same way. It is off until someone turns it on.

sections.title: When a Router May Accept Its Own Route
sections.content:
A router MAY accept a route whose ORIGINATOR_ID or NEXT_HOP matches its own, but only if all of these are true:

  • ACCEPT_OWN processing is enabled by configuration.
  • The route carries the ACCEPT_OWN community.
  • The route originated from a source VRF on the router, meaning a VRF whose configured Route Distinguisher equals the one in the route.
  • The route targets one or more destination VRFs on the router, found by inspecting its Route Targets.
  • At least one destination VRF differs from the source VRF.

A route MUST NOT ever be accepted back into its source VRF, even if it carries RTs that match that VRF.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks the sticker, checks the mail really came from one of its own rooms, and checks it is going to a different room. Only then does it keep it.

sections.title: Propagation and Configuration Control
sections.content:
ACCEPT_OWN only makes sense for routes that can be tied to a source VRF through the Route Distinguisher and to a target VRF through the Route Target list, such as VPN routes with SAFI 128. So it SHOULD NOT be attached to routes that cannot be associated with a source VRF, and it SHOULD NOT be propagated when routes are propagated into a VRF. If a route carrying it arrives in an address family where the source VRF cannot be looked up, the community MUST be discarded, and a message MAY be logged.

If ACCEPT_OWN is controlled by configuration, it MUST default to disabled. When disabled, the router MUST NOT apply the special acceptance rules, but SHOULD still apply the propagation rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker only belongs on the right kind of mail. If it turns up on the wrong kind, the router peels it off. And by default the router ignores the sticker entirely.

sections.title: Change to the Decision Process
sections.content:
If a speaker supports ACCEPT_OWN and is configured for it, one step is added to the BGP decision process, right after the LOCAL_PREF comparison: when comparing two routes for a destination, the route with the ACCEPT_OWN community is preferred.

Everything else in the decision process is unchanged. The step MUST only be used when choosing the best path among VPN-IP routes, and MUST NOT be used for imported IP routes inside a VRF. Its purpose is to let the paths re-advertised by the route reflector with ACCEPT_OWN win over other paths the speaker may have received.
sections.plainLanguage: When two routes compete, the one with the sticker wins, so the reflector's version is the one the router uses.

sections.title: Example: Local Extranet
sections.content:
The non-normative appendix shows an extranet. PE1 has VRF 1 (RD 1, RT 1) facing CE1 and VRF 2 (RD 2, RT 2) facing CE2, and connects to a route reflector (RR). PE1 learns prefix X from CE1 and advertises it to the RR with RD 1 and RT 1. The goal is to import X into VRF 2 and advertise it to CE2.

Without ACCEPT_OWN, PE1 would need its VRF 2 import RT or import policy changed, which is cumbersome in a large network. With it, the RR re-advertises X back to PE1 with RT 2 appended. PE1 accepts it, imports it into VRF 2 because of RT 2, and works out the adjacency rewrite within VRF 1 from the RD and prefix. RT 1 is ignored because it belongs to the source VRF. The same must happen in the other direction, all without changing PE1's BGP policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Two classrooms in one school want to share a note. Instead of rewriting each room's rules, the office stamps the note with the second room's name and sends it back.

sections.title: Scope, Security and IANA
sections.content:
ACCEPT_OWN is useful within a single autonomous system with a single layer of route reflectors. Use with hierarchical route reflectors or across autonomous systems needs further specification and is out of scope. The approach may also fit other technologies that give a speaker multiple routing contexts, with VRF, Route Distinguisher and Route Target read as the equivalent constructs.

On security, the extension lets a router's own prefix be advertised into a different VRF on that router. The RFC says such a route is like any other BGP route, shares its vulnerabilities, and does not change the underlying security issues of BGP VPN. IANA assigned 0xFFFF0001 in the BGP Well-known Communities registry.
sections.plainLanguage: This trick works for one network with one layer of helpers. It does not add new dangers beyond what BGP VPNs already have.
